Maladaptive Strategies.value: never allow myself to feel or express anger
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
issues.explanation: For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, revenge-focused ideation about identifiable responsible people is hard to reconcile unless there was clear culpability (e.g. negligence), which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It appears clinically mismatched to the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: Generalized threat from strangers and scanning faces for danger fit interpersonal assault or public violence better than a child's medical crisis. These threat items imply fear of hostile people in ordinary situations, but the rest of the profile does not provide a coherent bridge from the illness trauma to stranger-based danger expectations.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall could occur, but here it primarily supports the revenge item and interpersonal-threat theme. In combination with the stranger-threat items, it pulls the profile toward an assault/perpetrator formulation rather than a child's illness trauma formulation.

issues.item: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me
issues.explanation: Meaning seeking is not inherently maladaptive and, in this profile, sits awkwardly with the otherwise threat-trigger-memory driven formulation; it does not clearly function as an avoidance/safety strategy tied to the selected triggers, threat items, or memory pattern.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance for interpersonal threat in faces/body language is difficult to reconcile with the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is more plausibly linked to medical cues, loss cues, or signs of illness rather than hostile people.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Needing to stay alert to fall asleep implies ongoing external danger monitoring; for a trauma centered on a child's illness, this would usually require clearer linkage to caregiving/medical monitoring, which is absent from the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: For the indexed trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, 'anything that reminds me of someone I have lost' implies bereavement/loss rather than ongoing threat or illness trauma. That is a hard-to-explain mismatch unless the child died, which is not the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: Within the overall profile, the dominant theme is fear/hypervigilance/disorientation around threat cues (sirens, crying, startle, sleep vigilance, physical reactivity, confused/unreal memory). 'Intense rage' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the rest of the profile and sits awkwardly beside suppression of anger, making this item clinically less coherent than the others.

vignette:
Mateo was 25, a single Latin American man working as a data scientist, when he finally agreed to seek help for a trauma that had begun years earlier but still intruded on ordinary days. The event he described was his younger son's medical crisis, a period he still struggled to recount in a straight line because the memories refused to settle into sequence. He could tell the broad outline: the child had become suddenly and dangerously ill, and the family was thrust into hospitals, ambulances, and repeated physical examinations. Beyond that, the details came back in fragments. He remembered a corridor, harsh lights, the tight press of people moving quickly, and his own sense that time had split apart. Even now, he said, the story felt so extreme that it was hard to believe it had actually happened to him, as if it belonged to someone else.

When Mateo tried to describe those days, he often stalled on the order of events. He could recall pieces with vivid force, but not arrange them properly, and that confusion was part of what made talking about it so upsetting. He said that remembering the episode brought back the same terror he had felt then, not a dulled or distant version of it. He could feel his body reacting as he spoke, as though the crisis were happening again in the room with him. Certain moments were especially potent: the wail of sirens outside the hospital, the smell of sweat or body odour in crowded waiting areas, and crying. He did not describe crying as merely sad; it was a cue that instantly took him back to the period when his child's distress signaled danger and everything in him had braced for bad news. Sirens were particularly sharp triggers because they seemed to cut through whatever he was doing and drop him back into that earlier urgency. The smell of sweat or body odour was similarly loaded, linked in his mind to the overheated, tense atmosphere of medical spaces where he had spent long stretches waiting and fearing the worst.

After the illness, Mateo found himself organizing his life around the possibility of being overwhelmed by reminders. He tried hard not to think about what had happened, and when thoughts started intruding, he pushed them away quickly rather than let them develop. He also made a rule for himself that he would never allow himself to feel or express anger. He described that choice matter-of-factly, as something he had decided he had to do, though he could not say he felt free in that state. When asked about his daily routine, he gave examples of how carefully he managed medical cues. He avoided hospitals whenever possible, kept his distance from ambulances on the street, and became uneasy around physical examinations. Even routine appointments were difficult to arrange, and he tended to delay them unless absolutely necessary. In the period after the trauma, these patterns narrowed his world in practical ways, making some everyday tasks more complicated than they needed to be.

At work, Mateo's data science job offered structure, but it did not fully protect him from reminders. He noticed that ordinary sounds in the office or on his commute could make him jump in a way that embarrassed him. A door slamming, a chair scraping, or a sudden noise from the street could produce an immediate startle response that was out of proportion to what was happening around him. He had come to expect that he would need to stay alert even when nothing seemed wrong, and that vigilance made it hard to fall asleep at night. He would lie in bed scanning for sounds, listening for anything that might demand attention, and the effort of staying watchful often kept him awake longer than he wanted. When a trigger did catch him, his body could react strongly: his heart raced, his muscles tightened, and he felt physically jolted by the reminder. Those episodes left him drained and self-conscious, though he continued to keep most of it to himself.

By the time he came for treatment, Mateo was not describing dramatic outbursts or visible collapse. Instead, he spoke of a life organized around holding things in, steering away from reminders, and staying on guard. He had grown weary of being startled by ordinary sounds, of losing sleep because he could not relax, and of feeling dragged back into the terror of his child's illness by a siren passing outside or by the smell of sweat in a crowded place. What finally brought him in was the accumulation of all of it: the strain of keeping the memories at bay, the difficulty of being around medical settings, and the sense that he was still living with his body stuck in that earlier emergency. He said he wanted help because he was tired of feeling as if the worst moment of his life could be reactivated at any time, and because he hoped he might one day remember what happened without being thrown back into the same fear.
